explanation: The accounting equation is assets = liabilities + equity. It describes how recognised resources are financed by obligations and residual ownership. Every recorded transaction preserves this equality, although it may change several accounts within one side.
Equality is a bookkeeping constraint, not proof that every asset is recoverable or every obligation has been recognised correctly. Valuation, completeness and classification still require judgment.

types.name: Asset-financed change
types.explanation: A resource and matching obligation or equity arise.

types.name: Asset exchange
types.explanation: One asset replaces another.

types.name: Earnings change
types.explanation: Recognised income or expense changes equity.

workedCase.setup: A company starts with ₹100 lakh cash funded entirely by equity and buys a ₹30 machine with cash.
steps: Initially assets ₹100 = liabilities zero + equity ₹100.
After purchase, cash ₹70 + machine ₹30 = total assets ₹100.
Equity stays ₹100 because the purchase exchanges assets rather than immediately creating a ₹30 loss.
workedCase.result: The equation balances before and after the transaction.
workedCase.interpretation: Later depreciation, impairment or disposal can affect earnings; initial purchase treatment and subsequent expense recognition are different stages.

analysis: Reconcile totals without treating balance as evidence of economic accuracy.

explanation: Double-entry bookkeeping records equal total debits and credits for each transaction. It captures the relationship between resources, obligations and income instead of recording cash movements alone. A transaction may involve more than two accounts while still balancing.

Journal entries flow into account ledgers and ultimately financial statements. Errors can balance if the wrong account or amount appears on both sides, so reconciliations and supporting evidence remain necessary.

types.name: Simple entry
types.explanation: One debit and one credit.

types.name: Compound entry
types.explanation: Multiple debit or credit accounts.

types.name: Adjusting entry
types.explanation: Period-end recognition or correction without a new cash payment.

workedCase.setup: Buy equipment for ₹50 lakh, paying ₹20 cash and borrowing ₹30.
steps: Debit equipment ₹50.
Credit cash ₹20 and credit loan liability ₹30.
Total debits and credits both equal ₹50.
workedCase.result: The entry records the asset and both funding sources.
workedCase.interpretation: Cash-only bookkeeping would miss the ₹30 debt-funded investment and understate both equipment and obligations.

analysis: Reconcile entries with invoices, contracts and cash records.

explanation: Debit and credit identify the two sides of an account, not universal synonyms for good and bad or increase and decrease. Asset and expense accounts normally increase with debits; liability, equity and income accounts normally increase with credits. Contra-accounts can have the opposite normal balance.
A bank statement is written from the bank's perspective: your deposit is its liability. This explains why statement terminology may appear opposite to your own cash ledger.

types.name: Debit-normal accounts
types.explanation: Usually assets and expenses.

types.name: Credit-normal accounts
types.explanation: Usually liabilities, equity and income.

types.name: Contra-account
types.explanation: Offsets another account, such as accumulated depreciation.

workedCase.setup: A company makes a ₹10 lakh cash sale with no associated cost included in this isolated entry.
steps: Debit cash ₹10 to increase an asset.
Credit revenue ₹10 to recognise income.
If the sale was on credit, debit receivables instead of cash.
workedCase.result: The debit depends on the resource received, not whether the event is profitable.
workedCase.interpretation: Complete profit measurement also needs related costs and relevant revenue-recognition criteria.

analysis: Check contra-accounts and the reporting perspective.

explanation: Journals record transactions in chronological order; ledgers organise them by account. A trial balance lists ledger balances to check total debits against credits. Closing entries transfer temporary income and expense balances into the appropriate equity account for the next period.

A balanced trial balance does not detect omitted transactions, equal misstatements or posting to the wrong account. Financial statements need adjustments, reconciliations and measurement judgments beyond arithmetic equality.

types.name: Journal
types.explanation: Chronological transaction record.

types.name: Ledger
types.explanation: Account-level history and balance.

types.name: Trial balance
types.explanation: Debit-credit total check.

types.name: Closing process
types.explanation: Reset temporary accounts and update equity.

workedCase.setup: Assume revenue is ₹100 lakh and recognised expenses ₹70, with no distributions.
steps: Ledger balances produce ₹30 profit.
Close revenue and expense accounts for the reporting period.
Transfer the ₹30 result into retained earnings under the simplified equity presentation.
workedCase.result: Income accounts reset for the next period while cumulative equity carries forward.
workedCase.interpretation: Cash does not reset at year-end, because it is a continuing balance-sheet account.

analysis: Separate temporary accounts from permanent balances.

explanation: Cash accounting recognises activity when cash is received or paid. Accrual accounting recognises economic performance and obligations under the relevant criteria, even when cash moves in another period. Receivables, payables and deferrals connect the two timing systems.
Accrual profit helps describe activity, but estimates and recognition choices create judgment. Cash flow helps explain liquidity, yet an advance payment is not necessarily earned revenue.

types.name: Cash basis
types.explanation: Recognition follows cash movement.

types.name: Accrual basis
types.explanation: Recognition follows performance and obligation criteria.

types.name: Timing bridge
types.explanation: Receivables, accruals and deferrals reconcile differences.

workedCase.setup: A firm delivers a qualifying ₹20 lakh service in December and collects in January.
steps: Under the simplified accrual assumption, December records revenue ₹20 and receivables ₹20.
January records cash collection and reduces receivables.
Under cash recognition, the receipt appears in January instead.
workedCase.result: The same transaction has different period timing under the two bases.
workedCase.interpretation: Recognition is not chosen merely to smooth profit; the applicable reporting framework determines the criteria.

explanation: Revenue recognition asks when and how much consideration reflects satisfied obligations to customers. Expense recognition records resource consumption, obligations and losses under applicable rules; some costs enter asset balances before being expensed. Matching is useful intuition but does not override recognition requirements.
A customer invoice or cash receipt alone may not establish earned revenue. The contract, performance, variable consideration and principal-agent role can all matter.

types.name: Point-in-time revenue
types.explanation: Recognition when a qualifying transfer occurs.

types.name: Over-time revenue
types.explanation: Recognition as qualifying performance progresses.

types.name: Immediate versus allocated expense
types.explanation: Current recognition or consumption of a recognised asset.

workedCase.setup: A customer prepays ₹12 lakh for twelve equal months of service. Assume the service is provided evenly and qualifies for monthly recognition.
steps: On receipt, record cash ₹12 and a contract liability ₹12.
After one month, recognise revenue ₹1 and reduce the liability to ₹11.
Cash remains ₹12 before other spending.
workedCase.interpretation: Different contractual obligations or performance patterns require a different recognition schedule.

analysis: Distinguish cash, invoicing and recognised revenue.

explanation: Accruals recognise earned income or incurred expense before settlement. Deferrals postpone recognition of cash already received or paid. A prepayment is an asset for future service; a provision is an obligation with uncertain timing or amount when recognition criteria are met.
These accounts solve different timing and uncertainty problems. A provision is not a general reserve to create whenever management expects a difficult future year.

types.name: Accrued expense
types.explanation: Incurred cost not yet settled.

types.name: Prepayment
types.explanation: Payment for future benefit.

types.name: Deferred revenue
types.explanation: Cash received before earning it.

types.name: Provision
types.explanation: Recognised uncertain obligation.

workedCase.setup: Pay ₹12 lakh insurance covering twelve equal months. Assume one month has elapsed.
steps: Initially record prepayment ₹12.
Recognise expense ₹1 for the consumed month.
Closing prepayment is ₹11, before any other adjustments.
workedCase.result: Cash outflow is ₹12 while the month's expense is ₹1.
workedCase.interpretation: An unpaid earned salary would instead create an accrued liability; its accounting direction differs from a prepayment.

analysis: Identify whether cash precedes or follows performance.
Separate timing balances from uncertainty estimates.

explanation: Capital expenditure acquires or improves resources with qualifying benefits beyond the current period. Operating expenditure supports current operations or fails asset-recognition criteria. A capital payment is not automatically excluded from economic cost: depreciation and impairment may recognise its consumption later.
The distinction affects profit timing and cash-flow presentation. It must follow applicable rules and the nature of the expenditure rather than management's desire to increase EBITDA.

types.name: Capital acquisition
types.explanation: Purchase of a qualifying long-lived resource.

types.name: Operating cost
types.explanation: Current service or consumption.

types.name: Repair versus improvement
types.explanation: Maintenance compared with a qualifying enhancement.

workedCase.setup: A firm spends ₹100 lakh on a machine and ₹5 on ordinary maintenance. Assume the machine qualifies as an asset and lasts five years, with no residual value.
steps: Capitalise the ₹100 machine.
Annual straight-line depreciation is ₹20 under the simplified assumptions.
Expense ordinary maintenance ₹5 as incurred.
workedCase.result: First-year expense is ₹25 rather than the full ₹105 cash payment.
workedCase.interpretation: Different useful lives, residual values and component accounting change the schedule; classification does not eliminate the investment outflow.

analysis: Connect asset investment, depreciation and cash flow.

explanation: Capitalisation places a qualifying cost in an asset balance; immediate expensing reduces current earnings. Capitalised cost is later consumed through depreciation, amortisation, cost of sales or impairment. The economic expenditure may be identical even when recognition timing differs.

Improper capitalisation overstates current earnings and assets. Comparisons need to consider differences in policies and the underlying benefits rather than treating higher reported profit as automatically better performance.

types.name: Immediate expense
types.explanation: No qualifying future asset is recognised.

types.name: Capitalised asset
types.explanation: Recognised cost allocated to future periods.

types.name: Subsequent impairment
types.explanation: Reduction when the asset's carrying amount is not recoverable.

workedCase.setup: Assume a qualifying asset costs ₹30 lakh and is consumed evenly over three years, with no residual. Compare immediate expense for illustration only.
steps: Immediate expense would reduce first-year profit by ₹30.
Capitalisation followed by amortisation reduces profit by ₹10 each year.
Both treatments use ₹30 cash initially.
workedCase.result: Timing of profit differs while initial cash spending is unchanged.
workedCase.interpretation: Actual treatment is determined by the reporting rules, not an elective choice between these illustrations.

analysis: Identify the asset and future benefit.

explanation: Historical cost starts from the transaction amount and follows relevant allocation and impairment rules. Fair value measures a current market-participant exit price under its framework. Amortised cost uses effective-interest allocation and applicable credit-loss adjustments for eligible instruments.

Measurement bases answer different questions and can change profit volatility. A current market decline may affect a fair-valued instrument immediately, while an amortised-cost instrument follows a different recognition model.

types.name: Historical cost
types.explanation: Transaction-based measurement with subsequent adjustments.

types.name: Fair value
types.explanation: Current market-participant exit-price measurement.

types.name: Amortised cost
types.explanation: Effective-interest carrying-value model for qualifying instruments.

workedCase.setup: Buy a bond for ₹100 lakh. Its market value later becomes ₹95; assume no cash payment yet.
steps: A fair-value carrying amount reflects ₹95 under the relevant category.
An amortised-cost amount is calculated from the effective-interest schedule and applicable losses, not automatically reset to ₹95.
Determine where any recognised change appears under the actual classification.
workedCase.result: The same market price movement can affect reported balances differently.
workedCase.interpretation: Classification, credit risk and reporting rules must be established before inferring the earnings impact.

analysis: Separate market movement from credit loss.

explanation: Materiality concerns whether information could reasonably influence users' decisions. Prudence supports caution in uncertainty without deliberate bias. Consistency helps comparison, but justified policy changes can be necessary. Going concern assumes continuation when appropriate rather than forced liquidation.

Materiality depends on nature as well as size. A small related-party payment or covenant issue may matter greatly. Going-concern assessment considers obligations, cash forecasts and feasible funding, not just a positive profit figure.

types.name: Quantitative materiality
types.explanation: Magnitude relative to relevant measures.

types.name: Qualitative materiality
types.explanation: Nature or context makes an item influential.

types.name: Going-concern basis
types.explanation: Continued operation rather than liquidation accounting.

workedCase.setup: A ₹1 lakh error occurs in a company with ₹1,000 lakh revenue, but it changes compliance with a debt covenant.
steps: The error is only 0.1% of revenue.
Its effect on covenant compliance may alter lender rights and user decisions.
Investigate and assess disclosure or correction under the applicable framework.
workedCase.result: Small size alone does not establish immateriality.
workedCase.interpretation: There is no universal percentage that resolves every materiality judgment.

analysis: Assess continuity using realistic cash and funding evidence.

explanation: An estimate changes when new information revises a measurement, such as useful life or expected credit loss. A policy determines the accounting principle or basis used. An error reflects a mistake or misuse of information that should have been considered. These classifications can require different treatment.
Do not label an old mistake a new estimate merely to avoid correction. The governing framework determines when changes affect current and future periods or require retrospective treatment.

types.name: Estimate revision
types.explanation: New information changes an uncertain measure.

types.name: Policy change
types.explanation: A different accounting basis is applied.

types.name: Error correction
types.explanation: Previously available information was omitted or misused.

workedCase.setup: An asset has carrying value ₹60 lakh and three remaining years, with zero residual. New information supports five remaining years.
steps: Old annual depreciation would be ₹20.
Revised prospective depreciation is ₹60/5 = ₹12, assuming an estimate change.
If the original schedule instead resulted from a calculation mistake, assess error-correction rules.
workedCase.result: Similar numerical changes can have different accounting explanations.
workedCase.interpretation: Classification and supporting evidence matter more than the label management chooses.

explanation: Reporting periods define the interval for flows and the date for balances. Comparative statements show earlier periods to help users distinguish trend, seasonality and one-off effects. Different period lengths or business combinations can undermine direct growth comparisons.

Interim results may have seasonal patterns or special estimation requirements. Annualising one strong quarter can overstate sustainable activity; changes in classification or restatement should be reconciled before comparison.

types.name: Annual reporting
types.explanation: Full-year activity and year-end position.

types.name: Interim reporting
types.explanation: Shorter-period information.

types.name: Comparative or restated figures
types.explanation: Prior information shown consistently where required.

workedCase.setup: A retailer earns ₹40 lakh in a holiday quarter and ₹10 in each other quarter.
steps: Annual profit is ₹40 + ₹10 + ₹10 + ₹10 = ₹70.
Multiplying the holiday quarter by four would imply ₹160.
Compare the holiday quarter with the corresponding prior-year quarter and assess full-year seasonality.
workedCase.result: A short reporting interval need not represent a normal annual run rate.
workedCase.interpretation: Acquisitions and differing calendars can create additional comparability issues.

explanation: Standalone accounts describe one legal entity. Consolidated accounts present a parent and controlled subsidiaries as a group, eliminating internal transactions. A subsidiary's revenue is not added again through dividends received by the parent; consolidation avoids such double counting.
The group perspective does not erase legal barriers to cash movement. Parent debt may depend on dividends from subsidiaries, which can be constrained by law, contracts or minority interests.

types.name: Standalone
types.explanation: One legal entity's statements.

types.name: Consolidated
types.explanation: Controlled entities presented as one economic group.

types.name: Non-controlling interest
types.explanation: Other owners' interest in consolidated subsidiaries.

workedCase.setup: A parent sells goods to its subsidiary for ₹20 lakh; the subsidiary sells them outside the group for ₹30. Assume all goods are sold externally.
steps: Standalone records show the internal sale in the parent.
Consolidation removes the ₹20 internal revenue and corresponding internal purchase.
Group external revenue is ₹30, not ₹50.
workedCase.result: Only transactions with outside parties remain as group revenue.
workedCase.interpretation: Unsold internal inventory can also require eliminating unrealised group profit.

analysis: Assess parent cash access separately from group totals.

explanation: Ind AS, IFRS and US GAAP are reporting frameworks with related objectives but distinct rules, adoption settings and disclosure requirements. Similar account labels do not guarantee identical recognition or measurement. A financial comparison should identify the framework and reporting period before making adjustments.

Framework differences can affect development costs, inventory methods, impairment, leases and cash-flow classifications. Avoid assuming an IFRS illustration automatically describes every Indian or US issuer.

types.name: IFRS Accounting Standards
types.explanation: Standards issued by the IASB and adopted in relevant jurisdictions.

types.name: Ind AS
types.explanation: Indian standards with their own legal adoption and differences.

types.name: US GAAP
types.explanation: US accounting principles and authoritative requirements.

workedCase.setup: Two firms spend ₹10 lakh on development activity and report different current expenses.
steps: Identify each firm's framework and the nature of expenditure.
Check whether each firm's recognition criteria permit or require an asset.
Adjust analytical comparisons only after understanding subsequent amortisation and tax effects.
workedCase.result: A profit gap can reflect accounting differences rather than superior cash economics.
workedCase.interpretation: The example does not assert that all development spending qualifies under any framework.

analysis: Use current primary standards for specific recognition questions.

explanation: Annual reports combine statements, notes, management discussion, governance and other required disclosures. Interim reports provide updates between annual periods. Regulatory filings may contain timely events or additional detail not visible in a headline presentation.

Read audited numbers alongside accounting policies, commitments, risks and the audit opinion. A shareholder letter is a narrative source, not a substitute for reconciling financial statements and notes.

types.name: Annual report
types.explanation: Periodic comprehensive reporting package.

types.name: Interim report
types.explanation: Shorter-period financial update.

types.name: Event filing
types.explanation: Disclosure of specified developments.

types.name: Investor presentation
types.explanation: Management-selected communication.

workedCase.setup: Management highlights ₹100 lakh adjusted profit while the statement reports ₹70.
steps: Find the reconciliation of the ₹30 difference.
Identify whether adjustments are recurring, non-cash or genuinely unusual.
Read notes and cash-flow effects before using the adjusted number in valuation.
workedCase.result: A report's headline requires reconciliation with its underlying statements.
workedCase.interpretation: Audited reporting provides assurance within its scope, not a guarantee of future returns or absence of every error.

analysis: Trace alternative metrics to reported figures.
Check filing dates, scope and assurance.

explanation: Revenue describes consideration earned by transferring promised goods or services, rather than every receipt into a bank account. Begin with the customer contract: identify the promises, determine consideration, allocate it to distinct obligations, and recognise it as those obligations are satisfied. The applicable framework determines the exact recognition criteria.

A cash sale can create revenue and cash together. A credit sale creates revenue and a receivable first. An advance normally creates cash and a contract liability until performance occurs. This timing distinction explains why strong sales can coexist with weak cash collection. Other operating income should be examined by its nature; the label alone does not establish that it is comparable to core product sales.

types.name: Point-in-time revenue
types.explanation: Recognition occurs when the relevant control-transfer conditions are met, such as qualifying delivery of a product.

types.name: Over-time revenue
types.explanation: Recognition follows performance over time when the applicable criteria are met, using an appropriate progress measure.

types.name: Recurring and non-recurring sales
types.explanation: Subscriptions and repeat purchases may be more forecastable than isolated contracts; recurrence does not override recognition rules.

workedCase.setup: An illustrative company receives ₹12 lakh on 1 April for twelve months of evenly delivered service. Assume the service qualifies for over-time recognition and there are no taxes or refunds.
steps: Record ₹12 cash and ₹12 contract liability on receipt.
Recognise ₹1 revenue for each month of service delivered.
After three months, revenue totals ₹3 and the remaining contract liability is ₹9.
workedCase.result: Cash received is ₹12, but revenue earned to date is ₹3; the liability represents the remaining service obligation.
workedCase.interpretation: If the company spent the entire advance immediately, it would still owe nine months of service. Cash availability and completed performance therefore answer different questions.

analysis: Read the revenue-recognition policy and contract terms.
Separate price, volume, mix, timing and collectability as drivers.
Reconcile revenue to receivables, contract assets, advances and customer cash collections.

explanation: Accounting follows recognition, measurement and presentation. Start by asking whether the event creates an eligible asset, obligation, income, expense or owner transaction. Double-entry then records equal effects so the accounting equation remains balanced. A balanced entry can still be wrong if the event is invented, misclassified or measured improperly.

Accrual accounting separates service delivery and consumption from payment. Capitalisation stores qualifying cost in an asset until later consumption, while expensing recognises the cost now. IFRS, Ind AS and US GAAP share many principles but differ in particular rules; the relevant framework, country and reporting period must be stated.

types.name: Recognition
types.explanation: Determines whether and when an item belongs in the accounts.

types.name: Measurement
types.explanation: Determines the amount using the required cost, fair-value or other basis.

types.name: Presentation
types.explanation: Classifies the recognised amount within statements.

types.name: Disclosure
types.explanation: Explains policies, assumptions, risks and reconciliations beyond headline totals.

workedCase.setup: A firm receives ₹12 lakh on 1 January for twelve months of evenly delivered service. Assume recognition over time is appropriate.
steps: At receipt, increase cash ₹12 and record a contract liability ₹12.
After one month, recognise revenue ₹1 and reduce that liability ₹1.
Cash remains ₹12 before other payments, while recognised revenue is ₹1.
workedCase.result: The accounting equation balances at both dates without treating the whole receipt as immediately earned income.
workedCase.interpretation: Different timing of cash and recognition explains why journal entries must follow the economic promise rather than the bank statement alone.

analysis: Identify the economic event and governing framework.
Trace the entry into statements and notes.
